content.title: About
content.content: Broccoflower is a hybrid vegetable created by crossing broccoli and cauliflower. It looks like a cauliflower head with bright green florets. It is eaten raw, offering a mild nutty flavor and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoflower was first developed in the 1990s in the United States.
It combines the nutritional benefits of both parent vegetables – broccoli and cauliflower.
The vivid green color comes from high chlorophyll levels, enhanced by ample light during growth.
Broccoflower is often featured in culinary shows as an “exotic” vegetable.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Provides over 100 % of the daily value for vitamin C, which supports immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Broccoflower contains glucosinolates and carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: People allergic to broccoli, cauliflower, or other crucifers may react to broccoflower.

items.title: Hard-to-digest fibers
items.content: High fiber content can cause gas and bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with most fresh produce, residues may be present; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Broccoflower can be eaten raw in salads, thinly sliced in wraps, or added to smoothies. It can also be briefly blanched to soften the texture while retaining most nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator in an airtight container or a perforated bag. It stays fresh for 5–7 days. Discard if yellow spots or off‑odors develop.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tail is the meat taken from the tail end of a chicken. It has a delicate flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a tender texture. The tail is popular in Asian cuisines, especially in dishes that require quick stir‑frying or braising.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken tail contains less fat than most other chicken parts.
In several Asian countries the tail is considered a delicacy and is served fried or marinated.
The tail is often used to enrich broths, giving them a deep, savory taste.
Traditional Chinese medicine regards chicken tail as beneficial for bone and joint health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken tail provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with other chicken cuts, the tail has a lower proportion of saturated fat, making it a lighter option.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B3 and B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The tail supplies zinc and iron, important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry meat, including the tail.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Like any raw meat, chicken tail can harbor salmonella or campylobacter if not stored or cooked properly.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should limit intake, as purines can raise uric acid levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The tail can be fried, baked, braised, or steamed. It is often marinated in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic, then quickly stir‑fried until golden. Serve it as a snack, or add it to soups, stews, and noodle dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chicken tail in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for about 3 months. Discard any pieces that develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Dark chocolate candy (NFS, item 5088) are small sweets coated with chocolate that contains a high cocoa content (usually 70 % or more). They have an intense, slightly bitter flavor typical of dark chocolate and may include additions such as nuts, dried fruit, or spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chocolate contains more antioxidants than milk chocolate due to its higher cocoa solids.
Demand for "pure" dark chocolate with minimal additives grew by over 15 % in Europe during the 2020s.
High‑cocoa candies are often used in pastry making to impart a deep chocolate aroma.
Dark chocolate generally has a longer shelf life than milk chocolate when stored properly.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids in dark chocolate act as antioxidants, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium helps maintain normal muscle and nerve function and supports energy metabolism.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Dark chocolate stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, which can improve mood.

items.title: Lower sugar content
items.content: Candies with a high cocoa percentage usually contain less sugar than milk‑based counterparts.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Cocoa solids provide non‑heme iron, beneficial for individuals with iron deficiency.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cocoa components.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Dark chocolate is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Dark chocolate contains modest amounts of caffeine and theobromine, which can affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Heavy metal residues
items.content: Poor‑quality cocoa may contain trace amounts of lead or cadmium; choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dark chocolate candies can be enjoyed on their own, added to baked goods, sprinkled over ice cream, or used to make sauces for meat dishes. Let them sit at room temperature briefly to release their full aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place (15‑18 °C). For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator, but allow them to reach room temperature before eating to avoid condensation.

content.title: About
content.content: Haddock is a cold‑water marine fish of the cod family, found in the North Atlantic. When baked or broiled with a coating, it stays tender inside while the crust becomes crisp. The product is a staple in many European cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Haddock is one of the most popular fish in the United Kingdom, often served as part of "fish and chips".
Coatings can be made from breadcrumbs, flour, spices, or whole‑grain bread crumbs.
Haddock is high in protein and low in calories, making it a favorite among health‑conscious eaters.
In the wild, haddock migrate long distances, sometimes over 2,000 km, to find feeding grounds.
Smoked haddock, known as "finnan haddie," is a traditional Scottish delicacy.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Haddock provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, haddock contains very little fat, supporting a calorie‑controlled diet.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune function.

items.title: Contains omega‑3s
items.content: Haddock provides modest amounts of EPA and DHA, beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including haddock.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While haddock generally has low mercury levels, pregnant women and young children should limit intake.

items.title: Coating additives
items.content: Pre‑made coating mixes can contain excess salt, trans fats, or preservatives; choose simple, wholesome options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake haddock at 180‑200 °C for 15‑20 minutes, or pan‑broil until the crust is golden. Serve with lemon, fresh herbs, vegetable sides, or a light yogurt‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh haddock refrigerated at 0‑2 °C and use within 2 days, wrapped in plastic film. Frozen fillets store at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts (Arachis hypogaea) are the edible seeds of a plant native to South America. Although they are commonly called nuts, peanuts are legumes, related to beans and lentils. They have a rich, savory flavor and are eaten roasted, boiled, or ground into peanut butter and are used in cooking in many cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are legumes, not true tree nuts.
The plant flowers above ground, but the pods develop underground.
Peanuts originated in South America and spread around the world after European contact.
Peanut butter is one of the most popular peanut products.
Peanuts are also pressed to make peanut oil.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Peanuts provide a good amount of protein for a plant food.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Peanuts contain mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains niacin, folate, and vitamin E
items.content: These nutrients support energy metabolism, cell function, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Provides magnesium and fiber
items.content: These support normal muscle function and digestion.

items.title: Contains plant compounds
items.content: Peanuts contain polyphenols such as resveratrol, which has antioxidant properties.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut allergy is one of the more common and serious food allergies and can cause severe reactions. People with this allergy must avoid peanuts and check labels carefully.

items.title: Aflatoxin
items.content: Peanuts can be contaminated with aflatoxin, a toxin produced by mold, especially when stored improperly.

items.title: High in calories and added salt
items.content: Peanuts are calorie-dense, and salted or flavored varieties can be high in sodium.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole peanuts are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peanuts can be eaten roasted or boiled as a snack, added to salads, stir-fries, sauces, and baked goods, or ground into peanut butter. Choose unsalted or lightly salted peanuts and peanut butter without added sugar when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store shelled peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, or in the refrigerator for longer storage. Keep peanuts in the shell in a cool, dry place. Discard peanuts that look moldy, shriveled, or smell musty or rancid. Natural peanut butter is best refrigerated after opening.
